I disagree with the characterization that geopolitical events ultimately don’t matter much to the economy or markets. They absolutely do, especially when they affect energy, trade routes, commodities, and inflation. Oil is probably the clearest example. When geopolitical instability sends oil above $100, that doesn’t just mean higher prices at the gas pump. Energy is an input throughout the entire economy—transportation, manufacturing, agriculture, shipping, airlines, plastics, construction, etc. Those higher costs eventually work their way through to consumers, reduce purchasing power, squeeze corporate margins, and can keep inflation elevated. I also think simply pointing to a 4.1% unemployment rate and concluding that the labor market is healthy misses a lot of nuance. The headline unemployment rate doesn’t capture everyone who has left the labor force, people who are underemployed, or all of the difficulty people may be having finding comparable work. And as AI adoption accelerates, I think displacement in certain white-collar and administrative jobs could become a much larger issue than the headline unemployment number initially reflects. Then there’s the fiscal side. The national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion, deficits remain enormous, and investors are demanding increasingly high yields to finance that debt. The 10-year Treasury is flirting with 5%, while longer-term yields have already been above 5%. That matters tremendously. Higher yields raise the government’s interest expense, increase corporate borrowing costs, pressure equity valuations, and flow directly into things like mortgage rates, auto loans, and other consumer credit. If the Fed hikes again next week, that only adds additional pressure. Companies have to deal with higher financing costs and potentially lower valuation multiples, while consumers face higher borrowing costs and less disposable income. So I don’t think geopolitics, debt, oil, interest rates, and the labor market can be treated as background noise simply because stocks have historically gone up over long periods of time. Markets may absolutely continue higher, but these factors directly affect inflation, earnings, valuations, consumer spending, housing affordability, and ultimately economic growth. Ignoring them because they haven’t broken the market yet doesn’t mean they aren’t important.
